Komarow Osada Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Komarów-Osada, Poland

Not demolished. Komarów-Osada's Jewish community, present from soon after the town's founding in 1748, grew to 1,752 people (60 percent of the population) by 1921. Several dozen Jews were shot directly at this cemetery before the ghetto's liquidation, and in 1942 the Germans shot about 2,500 more in the fields outside town, burying them in mass graves. Between 1988 and 1995, at the initiative of Moris Trost — originally from Komarów-Osada and by then living in Frankfurt am Main — and other Jews, the cemetery was cleaned, planted with trees, and enclosed with a metal fence; the remains of several hundred people were exhumed from the nearby mass graves and reburied here, and four monuments along with dozens of new terrazzo matzevot were erected to commemorate specific families and Holocaust victims generally. A dozen or so recovered matzevot, the oldest from 1831, were also brought back to the site.
